vignette: At thirty-seven, Maya had not expected to be packing a bass guitar into its hard case for the last time. She was twenty-nine when the stage lights at a downtown indie venue flickered and died. She had been in the middle of a set, fingers still pressed to the strings, when a coordinated terrorist bombing tore through the brick wall behind the drum riser. The air instantly thickened with the acrid taste of burnt insulation and pulverized drywall. Before she could register the screaming, a second explosion blew the front doors inward, scattering the crowd into a chaotic panic of shattering glass and running feet. Her memories of the frightening event were very clear and detailed, down to the exact way the bass amplifier sparked and died. When the memory came back, it felt completely real across all her senses at once, and she could distinctly taste the copper and burnt insulation she had swallowed that night. In the months that followed, Maya found that the venue no longer felt like a place of music but a tomb waiting to reopen. Her body learned to scan every room for exits first and acoustics second. At the small rehearsal studio she now rented on the outskirts of the city, a dropped metronome or a sudden cymbal crash would spike her heart rate before her brain could register a harmless practice session. That jolt of physiological alarm did not simply pass; it pulled the scene forward. When her nervous system flared at the sharp crack of a dropped stick, she would suddenly feel or act as if the stressful experience were actually happening again. Maya would be standing on the stage, tasting the dust, watching the crowd scatter as if it were happening all at once, across every sense. The threat response became the key that unlocked the full sensory reliving, making the past impossible to keep at a distance. Each time the reliving returned, it cemented a new conviction: the world was fundamentally treacherous, and she no longer belonged anywhere in the community that gathered in enclosed spaces. She stopped answering calls from bandmates who wanted to book gigs, certain that people were not what they seemed and that crowds were just potential targets waiting for a detonator. But those very convictions did not protect her from the memories; they fed them. Maya's belief that she had no future and belonged nowhere created a hollow, hyper-vigilant space in her mind. Whenever she sat alone in her darkened apartment, waiting for a show that would never come, that hollow expectation acted like a beacon, drawing the traumatic memories to the surface with renewed intensity. The memories proved her fears right, and her fears guaranteed the memories would return. The loop drained her capacity to focus on sheet music or tune her instrument, and her irritability sharpened into abrupt anger outbursts that frightened her boyfriend, David. He tried to stay close, but Maya's distrust made his quiet reassurances feel like pressure, and his well-meaning invitations to public concerts only tightened her chest. Eventually, the strain of performing through the mental static became unsustainable. She packed her bass into its case, told David she needed time, and walked into a community mental health clinic last Tuesday. She does not know if she will ever play again, and she is terrified that stepping into the room will force her to relive the night the lights went out. What she hopes for, quietly, is a way to stop tasting copper when she hears a door slam and to believe, even for a moment, that she might actually have a future.
